lead: Overriding lets a subclass replace a parent method with its own body. Python does not guess which body to run: it scans a fixed list of classes, the method resolution order (MRO), and takes the first match. In a diamond, where two parents share one grandparent, the MRO and super() make each class run once. You need this to read library code, to combine mix-in classes, and to predict the output of inheritance questions in exams.
prereq: You need: 4.4 Inheritance, where a subclass reuses a parent class and super() calls the next class in the MRO.

blocks.text: A subclass may define a method with the same name as a parent method. For subclass objects the subclass body runs; the parent method is shadowed, not deleted. This is method overriding.
Account.withdraw(amount) moves money out. SavingsAccount(Account) overrides withdraw to check a minimum balance first, then calls super().withdraw(amount). Account().withdraw still uses the old body.
Matching is by name only; the parameter list does not matter. A subclass method with different parameters still overrides. super() searches the next class in the MRO, not just the direct parent.

Use it when the operation is the same but the rule differs: a savings account and a fixed deposit both expose interest(), at different rates. 4.6 covers how the call site then picks the right body at runtime.

Each class stores its lookup order in a tuple named __mro__. For the figure, D.__mro__ is (D, B, C, A, object). Python builds it by C3 linearization. Two rules matter: a class comes before its parents, and the bases keep their left-to-right order.
Lookup scans the tuple left to right, stops at the first class that has the name, and raises AttributeError if no class has it.
B comes before C because D(B, C) lists B first. A comes after both as their shared parent and appears once only. Write D(C, B) instead and the order becomes D, C, B, A, object.
object is the root of every class, so it is last in the chain.
D inherits B and C; both inherit A. That shape is the diamond problem: a naive depth-first walk of the parents reaches A twice, so A's state is set twice.

super() prevents it. super() means "the next class after the current one in the object's MRO", not "my parent". Inside B, the class after B is C, so super() reaches C; then C's super() reaches A. A runs once, last.

This is cooperative multiple inheritance. Each __init__ does its own work and calls super().__init__() so the chain continues. Every class in the chain must call it; one class that skips it silently cuts off the rest.
Mix-ins use this: LoggingMixin, RetryMixin, small classes adding one behaviour, combined with a real base class. Pass keyword arguments along the chain so each class takes what it needs.

figure.caption: D inherits B and C, and both inherit A. The MRO of D is D, B, C, A, object, so B is searched before C and the shared parent A is searched once.

spec.aria: Diamond inheritance with D inheriting B and C, both inheriting A; the MRO of D is D, B, C, A.

examples.question: Classes A, B(A), C(A) and D(B, C) each append their class name to self.order inside __init__ and then call super().__init__(). D first sets self.order to ['D']. Write the four classes, give the MRO of D, and state the value of d.order after d = D().
steps: MRO of D: read D.__mro__, giving D, B, C, A, object.
d = D() enters D.__init__, sets self.order = ['D'] and calls super().__init__().
Next class after D is B: B appends 'B', order becomes ['D', 'B'], then calls super().__init__().
Next class after B is C, not A: C appends 'C', order becomes ['D', 'B', 'C'], then calls super().__init__().
Next after C is A: A appends 'A', order becomes ['D', 'B', 'C', 'A'].
examples.answer: d.order is ['D', 'B', 'C', 'A'] and the MRO of D is D, B, C, A, object, so A ran exactly once, after C.

traps: Assuming super() calls the direct parent. In a diamond it calls the next class in the MRO, so A runs after C, once, not twice.
Assuming a different parameter list stops overriding. Python matches methods by name only.
Forgetting super().__init__() in one class of the chain: the classes after it never run, and no error is raised.
Swapping the bases to class D(C, B) and expecting the same MRO. It changes to D, C, B, A, object.
Thinking object comes first in the MRO, or that the shared parent A appears twice.

quiz.q: What does D.__mro__ contain for the figure?
quiz.a: (D, B, C, A, object): class names in lookup order, ending with object.

quiz.q: Why does super() inside B call C in the diamond?
quiz.a: super() follows the MRO of the object's class; C is the class after B there, not the direct parent A.

quiz.q: Classes P, Q(P), R(P), S(Q, R). Each __init__ appends its letter to self.order then calls super().__init__(); S sets order to ['S'] first. Give s.order.
quiz.a: MRO is S, Q, R, P, object, so the list is ['S', 'Q', 'R', 'P'].

quiz.q: Give the MRO of class Z(Y, X) where Y(X) and X(object).
quiz.a: Z, Y, X, object: bases in listed order, shared ancestor next, object last.

quiz.q: X.show() prints 'X'. Y(X) overrides show(), printing 'Y' then calling super().show(). State the output of Y().show() and why.
quiz.a: It prints Y then X on separate lines, because super() finds X's show in Y's MRO and calls it once.

quiz.q: A class Chain has parents M1, M2, both inheriting Base. M2's __init__ does not call super().__init__(). Which class never initialises, and is an error raised?
quiz.a: Base never initialises, because the chain stops at M2; no error is raised, which is why the bug is easy to miss.

beyond: Not for the exam. The C3 linearization rule first appeared in the Dylan language and is now the standard answer to the diamond problem. Django's class-based views and many Python libraries are built from deep mix-in chains, so reading an MRO is a daily skill in web work. Search next for "Python MRO", "C3 linearization" and "cooperative multiple inheritance". Metaclasses and __init_subclass__ build on the same lookup rules and sit outside this unit.
